title: Proofs in Geometry: The Angle Sum of a Triangle
summary: Axioms and theorems, how a proof is written (given, to prove, construction, proof, conclusion), and the proof that the angles of a triangle add up to 180°.

p: An axiom (or postulate) is a statement that we accept as true without proof, such as 'the shortest distance between two points is a straight line'. A theorem is a statement that is not obvious, but that we can prove using logic and axioms. This week we learn to write a proper proof.

sections.h: How to set out a proof
p: Step 1, Given: the information you start with. Step 2, To prove: what you want to show. Step 3, Construction: any line you add to the diagram (if needed). Step 4, Proof: a step-by-step argument with a reason for every statement. Step 5, Conclusion: finish with a closing statement, often Q.E.D. (from Latin, 'which was to be shown').

sections.h: Theorem 1: the angles of a triangle add up to 180°
p: Given: a triangle ABC. To prove: angle A + angle B + angle C = 180°. Construction: through A draw a line XY parallel to BC.
The picture shows the line XY drawn through A. The angle at X side equals angle B, and the angle at Y side equals angle C. Together with angle A they make a straight line.

img.alt: Triangle ABC with a line XY drawn through A parallel to BC, showing the alternate angles equal to B and C
img.cap: The line XY through A is parallel to BC.

p: Example 1: a triangle has angles 2x, 3x and 40°. Find x. The sum is 180°: 2x + 3x + 40 = 180, so 5x = 140 and x = 28°. The angles are 56°, 84° and 40°; check: 56 + 84 + 40 = 180.
Example 2: one angle of a triangle is 90°. The other two are x and 2x. Then x + 2x = 90, so x = 30°. The angles are 30°, 60° and 90°.
Example 3: the angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. The sum of the ratio parts is 9, so one part is 180° ÷ 9 = 20°. The angles are 40°, 60° and 80°.
Example 4: can a triangle have angles 50°, 60° and 80°? Add them: 50 + 60 + 80 = 190, which is not 180. So no.

title: The Exterior Angle of a Triangle
summary: What an exterior angle is, the exterior angle theorem and its proof, and worked examples.

p: If you extend one side of a triangle, you form an angle outside the triangle. This is the exterior angle. In the picture, side BC is extended to D, and the exterior angle is angle ACD.

img.alt: Triangle ABC with BC extended to D, showing the exterior angle ACD equal to angle A plus angle B
img.cap: The exterior angle ACD equals angle A plus angle B.

p: The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles. Given: triangle ABC with BC extended to D. To prove: angle ACD = angle A + angle B.

Statement 1: angle A + angle B + angle ACB = 180°. Reason: the angles of a triangle add up to 180° (Theorem 1). Statement 2: angle ACD + angle ACB = 180°. Reason: angles on a straight line BCD add up to 180°. Statement 3: so angle A + angle B + angle ACB = angle ACD + angle ACB. Reason: both equal 180°. Statement 4: subtract angle ACB from both sides: angle A + angle B = angle ACD. Q.E.D.

Example 1: in a triangle, two angles are 50° and 70°. The exterior angle at the third corner is y. By the theorem, y = 50° + 70° = 120°. Another way: the third angle is 180° − 50° − 70° = 60°, and y = 180° − 60° = 120°.

Example 2: in triangle PQR, angle P = 2x, angle Q = 3x, and the exterior angle at R is 140°. By the theorem, 140° = 2x + 3x, so x = 28°. Then angle P = 56°, angle Q = 84°, and angle R inside = 180° − 140° = 40°. Check: 56 + 84 + 40 = 180.
Example 3: the exterior angle of a triangle is 110° and one of the interior opposite angles is 40°. The other is 110° − 40° = 70°.

activity: The exterior angle of a triangle is 125° and one interior opposite angle is 55°. Find the other interior opposite angle and the interior angle next to the exterior angle. (Answers: 70° and 55°.)

title: Riders: The Angle Toolbox
summary: The angle facts you need to solve riders: straight lines, points, vertically opposite angles, parallel lines (Z, F, C patterns), and triangle facts.

p: A rider is a geometry problem that needs a chain of reasoning from theorems you know, to find an angle or to prove something. Think of yourself as a detective. Every step must have a reason.

sections.h: Angle facts to learn by heart
p: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Angles at a point add up to 360°. Vertically opposite angles (formed when two lines cross) are equal.

When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, three pairs of angles are related. Alternate angles are equal (the Z pattern). Corresponding angles are equal (the F pattern). Co-interior (allied) angles add up to 180° (the C pattern).

img.alt: Three diagrams of parallel lines cut by a transversal showing the Z pattern with equal alternate angles, the F pattern with equal corresponding angles and the C pattern with co-interior angles adding up to 180 degrees
img.cap: The Z, F and C patterns for parallel lines.

p: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides (the base angles) are equal. In an equilateral triangle all three angles are 60°. The angles in a right-angled triangle other than the right angle add up to 90°.

Write the reason for every step. Mark every angle you find on the diagram. Look for parallel lines, straight lines, isosceles triangles and vertically opposite angles. If you are stuck, find any angle you can and then use it.

title: Congruent Triangles, Polygons, Parallelograms and the Intercept Theorem
summary: The four conditions for congruent triangles, angles in polygons, properties of parallelograms and the intercept theorem.

p: Two triangles are congruent if they are exactly the same shape and size. You can prove it if one of these four conditions is true: SSS (three sides equal), SAS (two sides and the angle between them equal), ASA (two angles and the side between them equal), RHS (a right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side equal). In SAS the angle must be between the two sides, and in ASA the side must be between the two angles.

Opposite sides are equal and parallel. Opposite angles are equal. Adjacent angles add up to 180°, so if angle A = 100° then angle B = 80°. The diagonals bisect each other. A rhombus is a parallelogram with all four sides equal.

The sum of the interior angles of a polygon with n sides is (n − 2) × 180°. The sum of the exterior angles of any polygon is always 360°. In a regular polygon all sides and angles are equal, so one exterior angle = 360° ÷ n and one interior angle = 180° minus the exterior angle.
Example: a regular nonagon (n = 9). The sum of interior angles = 7 × 180° = 1260°. One interior angle = 1260° ÷ 9 = 140°. One exterior angle = 360° ÷ 9 = 40°. Check: 140° + 40° = 180°.

More: a regular pentagon has interior angle (3 × 180°) ÷ 5 = 108°. A polygon with an interior angle sum of 900° has n − 2 = 5, so n = 7 sides. A regular polygon with exterior angle 30° has 360 ÷ 30 = 12 sides.

If three or more parallel lines cut two transversals, they divide the transversals in the same ratio. In the simplest case, if the parallel lines cut off equal pieces on one transversal, they cut off equal pieces on the other. For example, equally spaced parallel lines divide any line crossing them into equal parts.

activity: A regular polygon has an exterior angle of 24°. How many sides does it have, and what is each interior angle? (Answers: 15 sides; 156°.)

title: Solving Riders: Worked Examples
summary: Three worked riders using parallel lines, polygons and a proof that a parallelogram with a bisected angle is a rhombus.

sections.h: Rider 1: parallel lines and a triangle
p: Two parallel lines AB and CD are cut by a straight line EF. EF meets AB at G and CD at H, with E above G and F below H. Angle EGB = 65°. Find angle GHD, angle BGH and angle AGH.
Angle GHD = 65°. Reason: it corresponds to angle EGB (corresponding angles, AB parallel to CD).
Angle BGH = 180° − 65° = 115°. Reason: angles on the straight line EGH add up to 180°.
Angle AGH = 65°. Reason: it is vertically opposite to angle EGB.
Check habit: opposite angles at a crossing are equal; angles along a line add to 180°.

A regular polygon has 9 sides. (a) Sum of interior angles = (9 − 2) × 180° = 1260°. (b) One interior angle = 1260° ÷ 9 = 140°. (c) One exterior angle = 360° ÷ 9 = 40°. Check: 140° + 40° = 180°. And 9 × 40° = 360°.

sections.h: Rider 3: prove that the parallelogram is a rhombus
p: Given: parallelogram ABCD in which the diagonal AC bisects angle DAB. To prove: ABCD is a rhombus (all four sides equal).

Proof. Angle DAC = angle CAB (call each x), because AC bisects angle DAB (given). AB is parallel to DC, so angle DCA = angle CAB = x (alternate angles). So angle DCA = angle DAC = x. In triangle ADC the angles at A and C are equal, so the triangle is isosceles and DA = DC (sides opposite equal angles are equal). But in a parallelogram AB = DC and AD = BC (opposite sides are equal). So AB = BC = CD = DA. So ABCD is a rhombus. Q.E.D.

Given: triangle ABC with AB = AC, and D is the midpoint of BC. Prove that triangles ABD and ACD are congruent. AB = AC (given). BD = DC (D is the midpoint). AD is common to both triangles. So the triangles are congruent by SSS. It follows that angle B = angle C and angle ADB = angle ADC = 90°.

activity: Try this rider. In triangle ABC, AB = AC and angle A = 40°. Find angles B and C, and say why they are equal. (Answers: 70° each, base angles of an isosceles triangle.)

title: Trigonometric Ratios: Sine, Cosine and Tangent
summary: The sides of a right-angled triangle, the ratios sine, cosine and tangent, SOH CAH TOA, and worked examples.

p: The word comes from the Greek trigonon (triangle) and metron (measure). Trigonometry studies the connection between the sides and the angles of triangles. It was developed by Greek, Indian and Arab mathematicians for astronomy, navigation and building. Today it is used in engineering, physics, computer graphics and GPS.

sections.h: The sides of a right-angled triangle
p: A right-angled triangle has one angle of 90°. Choose one of the other angles and call it θ (theta). The hypotenuse (HYP) is the longest side, always opposite the 90° angle. The opposite (OPP) is the side opposite θ. The adjacent (ADJ) is the side next to θ that is not the hypotenuse. If you change to the other acute angle, the opposite and adjacent sides swap over.

img.alt: A right-angled triangle with the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides labelled for the angle theta, and the memory aid SOH CAH TOA
img.cap: The three sides, and SOH CAH TOA.

sections.h: The three ratios: SOH CAH TOA
p: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse (SOH). cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse (CAH). tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent (TOA). These ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle.
In triangle PQR, angle Q = 90°, PQ = 5 cm and QR = 12 cm. Find PR, sin P, cos P and tan R.
PR² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169, so PR = 13 cm (Pythagoras).
For angle P: opposite = QR = 12, adjacent = PQ = 5, hypotenuse = 13. So sin P = 12/13 and cos P = 5/13.
For angle R: opposite = PQ = 5, adjacent = QR = 12. So tan R = 5/12.

A right-angled triangle has a hypotenuse of 15 cm and an angle of 35°. Find the side x next to the 35° angle. Relative to 35°, x is the adjacent side and 15 is the hypotenuse. We have A and H, so use CAH: cos 35° = x/15. So x = 15 × cos 35° = 15 × 0.8192 = 12.29 cm.
To find an angle you need two sides. Label the sides for the angle. Choose the ratio that uses them. Write the equation. Then use the inverse button on your calculator (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹).
Which ratio? Have H and O: sin. Have H and A: cos. Have O and A: tan. To find a side: angle and H, want O: sin. Angle and H, want A: cos. Angle and O, want A: tan. Angle and A, want O: tan.

activity: A right-angled triangle has opposite = 3 cm and hypotenuse = 5 cm. Find the angle. (Use sin θ = 3/5 = 0.6, so θ = sin⁻¹ 0.6 = 36.9°.)
